Matt Erickson: Yeah, absolutely — and it's probably spread across multiple departments to get all the data. You're inside a Class 1, Division 1 booth — it's white, bright lights, noises, a stressful environment. You're trying to say, 'How long was that soak?' 'I don't know, about five minutes.' But five minutes to you might actually be two minutes — the relativity of time. Even if you're very systematic about writing things down, if it's the wrong metric, you can't standardize or optimize anything from it. And if you're running a bunch of socks over an eight- or ten-hour shift, how many minutes are being lost that just aren't realistic? Then someone collects that 'precise' data that says five minutes every single time, when in reality it's two minutes, three minutes forty-seven seconds, four minutes. Bryan Fields: Right. I understand the goal and intention of a standardized SOP, but the starting material is a plant, and a plant means variables. As the chiller runs through its day it's not holding that exact same temperature — it's a moving variable. So having a standardized SOP against moving variables feels nearly impossible. What do you think about that?

Matt Erickson: You could go into the weeds and optimize to the ultimate degree, but it comes back to cost-benefit analysis. If we're chasing 3% more efficiency and it's costing us the equivalent of, say, a hundred dollars to chase ten dollars of value, it's probably not worth chasing — unless there's a way to change that math. It comes back to understanding what we're optimizing for, and that might change lot to lot, facility to facility, month to month. If you understand the cost-benefit analysis and what you're optimizing for based on the time of year or product type, you can make more informed decisions.

Bryan Fields: Is that where ingredient-based manufacturing comes into play — giving up certain elements of the process because you want to standardize, saying, 'We understand we might lose a little here, but if the end product is as consistent as possible, that's our overarching goal'?

Matt Erickson: Ingredient-based manufacturing, or ingredient-based formulation, in our opinion at Evolved, is the future of extraction. Let's use live resin vape carts as an example. If we're making live resin vape carts with a traditional hydrocarbon extraction system, we're tailoring the whole extraction process to optimize for that one specific output — but there are a ton of variables in the biomass and the process that go into making that cart. When we separate extraction — the actual process of pulling out the key ingredients — from manufacturing the end product, we focus on making two ingredients instead of one finished product: THCA crystals and HTE, high terpene extract. In a lot of markets there was a buzz around THC isolate — it commanded a high price, supply flooded in, and the price per gram dropped, so a lot of people wrote it off as a flash in the pan. But the real value proposition of isolating THCA at scale is ingredient-based manufacturing. Extraction's job becomes optimizing to make two ingredients — 99.9% THCA, and HTE — essentially everything else of value in the crude. With those two ingredients we can formulate any solvent-based concentrate to a super tight specification. THCA is THCA, whether it came from the best biomass or complete 'boof' material. So we can use lower-cost biomass to build up large quantities of THCA, and run smaller quantities of high-quality, connoisseur-type biomass just to get the HTE fraction, which is what differentiates strains. If we separate those two things and formulate on demand, it does some pretty incredible things for the business. First, it segments workflows — extraction only has to focus on extracting two ingredients, without worrying as much about biomass variability, while formulation works on a completely different cadence to make connoisseur-type products to a very tight spec. As rescheduling and APIs and standardization of end products come online, we can formulate very specifically to meet new regulations while also delivering a consistent brand experience — week over week, month over month, state to state. The other piece is profitability — mixing lower-valued THCA with higher-valued HTE to make the exact same product means your cost per gram is way lower than competitors who don't have that technology. You either make more profit while margins are high, or you can ride the price compression all the way down.

Bryan Fields: Let me reiterate to make sure I understand. Instead of having all these competing variables and moving targets, your team suggests simplifying extraction's job to two specific products — nail those two consistently, and the next team's job is to take those consistent inputs and hand off something equally consistent, almost like a gated structure from step zero to step one to step two. How does that differ from how teams operate today?

Matt Erickson: Today, if that live resin has to come out consistent like it has for months, the extraction tech has to optimize for efficiency and throughput in a commercial environment while also taking the time to make sure it comes out right — deciding whether to reprocess, whether changes are needed. It's added complexity, especially for a higher-end, connoisseur-type product, where it's less about throughput and efficiency and more like a chef working with ingredients, formulating, playing with different combinations, creating new products. One thing we haven't mentioned is that formulation lets you pivot. Market demand changes — everybody wants one product, then suddenly nobody does. If you're sitting on 50,000, 100,000, 300,000 vape carts you made based on a forecast, the only way to compete when demand shifts is dropping your price. Whereas if you're formulating on demand, very quickly, to a tight spec, you can shift as soon as demand shifts. You can even front-run trends — release a limited run of something, see how it does, and scale up if it picks up — without interrupting your extraction workflow at all. You can make one month's worth at a time instead of three, so nothing oxidizes sitting on a cart too long.

Bryan Fields: You're kind of eliminating the bullwhip effect — isolating the extraction team to that small, controlled environment you described, letting them focus on doing their one job really well, and then it's the next person's role to take it from there. Versus what probably happens now — sales comes back saying a product is flying off the shelves, resources get diverted, and by the time product comes through the pipeline, the demand has shifted and you're stuck discounting a huge backlog. Based on what you said, some teams are probably thinking, 'Matt, it's not that easy.' What are they missing? What's the biggest unlock for them to get there?

Matt Erickson: Usually there's resistance, especially around a well-established SKU — 'this is how we've always done it, it's not broken, we're not going to fix it.' Sometimes you can't get past that. So we start by offering THCA separation using our controlled crystallizer as another product line — maybe for infused pre-rolls or something else. As they get more comfortable having these two ingredients and playing with formulation, they start asking why they were ever doing it the harder way. We like to think of it almost like an assembly line — you don't have the same person walking a car through every single step. You want specialized, optimized functions handing off the baton.

Bryan Fields: Stop me if I'm wrong, but this seems to be leading toward what the FDA might want — more pharmaceutical-style manufacturing. Is continued verification part of the process — validating the HTE and THCA, testing to confirm they've met a quality threshold before moving on?

Matt Erickson: Absolutely, in some cases — not every group does it, but you have the ability to analyze those ingredients before they even go into a product, and then validate the finished product as well. If you look at pharmaceuticals, they isolate by crystallization — nobody's distilling, because distillation adds heat and a bunch of variables, it's not as pure, not as fast, and there's a lot of post-processing. Distillate has a place, but isolation gives you a much purer form, which gives you the versatility to formulate, and it also captures a completely new revenue stream — the terpenes, which are the differentiator between strains — that in some cases can be worth more than the cannabinoids themselves.

Bryan Fields: And the simplification probably unlocks real economic clarity too — true visibility into your actual COGS, because with that clean handoff from ingredient to ingredient, you know exactly what your costs were, what the market value of the output was, and as prices move up or down, exactly where you need to be to stay profitable.

Matt Erickson: Yeah, it shortens the feedback loop — you get more data sooner, so you can make adjustments on the fly and pivot. Agility is extremely important in any market, but especially one that's still relatively in its infancy — the established cannabis industry is what, fifteen years old? Markets and consumer demand are constantly changing, so having the ability to optimize for the reality on the ground is critical.

Bryan Fields: What becomes dangerous when companies copy and paste SOPs or workflows from other facilities?

Matt Erickson: Not understanding the why. There are generalized SOPs that most people can agree on in terms of what should and shouldn't be done for, say, a hydrocarbon system — but you're not going to run a tight operation off generalized SOPs. We want to make things very specific, with a clear understanding of why we're doing them. If you can't answer the why, get curious about it — is this step irrelevant, or is there a reason behind it? What happens if we don't do it? Maybe we're missing a different step that should replace it.

Bryan Fields: What about teams thinking about swapping or upgrading extraction equipment to increase throughput or efficiency? What proof should they ask for before writing a check?

Matt Erickson: About half of our work at Evolved is integration — using existing infrastructure wherever there's an opportunity. We also do full turnkey builds from the ground up, tailored to the client. Really it comes down to understanding what we're trying to optimize for and whether it's actually going to work. There's been a lot of best-case-scenario, bold claims from equipment manufacturers in extraction, so we built a demo facility where people can come see the technology actually work — partly to put our money where our mouth is, and partly so we can keep iterating and optimizing. A lot of that optimization is process optimization, which we continually share with clients — 'we tweaked this and we're getting way better crystallization efficiency, give it a try' — or clients come to us with a specific challenge they can't solve, and we try to replicate it in our skunkworks lab and find a solution, which also helps us understand real-world problems that need solving.

Bryan Fields: That's a great example — a team running a specific strain through a specific SOP gets certain results and asks you to help find the leak. Having that facility lets you diagnose and replicate the exact issue. I'd imagine other teams have called a vendor and said, 'You sold me this equipment with these specs, and it's nowhere near that,' and the vendor says, 'well, those are just ranges.'

Matt Erickson: Right — and to be fair to them, how would they even solve that problem if they don't have the capability? A lot of times it's not that they don't want to help, it's that they can't — they don't have the information to help. It comes back to the cookie-cutter extraction system, designed once and sold a hundred times. It might work great in a lot of applications, but for a new application or something they're trying to do differently, it doesn't work well — and going back to the manufacturer, they'll say, 'well, that's not what it was designed to do.'

Bryan Fields: Do you still see teams making purely economic decisions — comparing a cheaper band-aid option against a bigger investment — and actually thinking through the implications of sunk capex versus upgrading?

Matt Erickson: Definitely, there's a sunk cost fallacy, but that's part of the beauty of being able to do either. We start every conversation by understanding what the group is trying to accomplish, then present a phased approach to upgrading existing equipment — this is your current bottleneck, we tackle that, it shifts the bottleneck here, we tackle that — compared against a fresh build. We want groups to understand what's possible, because a lot of the time they think 'my extractor just doesn't work like that,' and the answer is, 'you're right, it doesn't — but we can make it work like that, would that be helpful?' We're always asking what's next, trying to get ahead of reactive problem-solving and take a more proactive approach, anticipating regulatory changes and hurdles before they hit.

Bryan Fields: Are there ROI numbers teams see and say, 'come on, there's no way we can hit these,' that help people visualize how a smaller investment versus a big expensive build can remove a huge leak?

Matt Erickson: There's been situations where we say, 'we'll double your throughput, increase your efficiency, and add crystallization on the back end,' and people are skeptical because they've been sold everything before. We have calculators and tools, but we always preface them as a guide, not gospel, and invite people to our demo facility to actually see it work. That unlocks a collaborative dynamic — 'oh, I see how you did this, would this work?' — and being able to show our work before they make a financial commitment is extremely powerful.

Bryan Fields: I'm sure that's very influential going forward. I can imagine some teams have said, 'Matt, if these numbers are real, why don't you pay for the install and we'll do a revenue split?'

Matt Erickson: Yeah, we've talked about that. Groups ask for a discount, and we ask, 'do you want to do a rev split instead?' Once you break down the numbers, they realize a rev split would be way more expensive than any discount — which is exactly the point. Bryan Fields: Matt, last question for our listeners — what question do you wish more people asked you?

Bryan Fields: I love it. For our listeners who want to get in touch and solve their extraction problems, where can they find you?

Matt Erickson: Yeah, absolutely. Thanks, Bryan.
summary: In this episode, Matt Erickson breaks down why chasing raw extraction throughput can quietly destroy profitability, and argues that operators should instead optimize for the specific cost-benefit math of their own business — balancing throughput, efficiency, and output quality. He introduces ingredient-based manufacturing, a model that separates extraction into producing two standardized ingredients (THCA isolate and high terpene extract) which can then be formulated on demand into consistent, scalable end products, giving operators pricing flexibility, brand consistency across markets, and the agility to pivot with shifting consumer demand. The conversation is a practical guide for extraction operators and MSOs on diagnosing hidden inefficiencies, avoiding cookie-cutter equipment traps, and building systemized, scalable processes instead of relying on one person's tribal knowledge.
takeaways: Throughput measures activity, not performance — maximizing biomass processed per shift can mask falling extraction efficiency and output quality, hurting overall profitability.
Operators should run a cost-benefit analysis specific to their own business model (large MSO vs. small connoisseur producer) rather than copying generic KPIs like 'socks processed per day.'

Separating extraction from formulation lets companies use lower-cost biomass for THCA while reserving premium biomass only for terpene extraction, lowering COGS and increasing margin.
Formulating on demand allows brands to avoid overproduction, oxidized shelf product, and forced discounting, while enabling them to front-run trends with limited-batch releases.
Standardization should apply to the process and the understanding behind it (the 'why'), not to rigid, cookie-cutter equipment — equipment should be customized, process should be standardized.
A business is only truly scalable if operational knowledge lives in documented, understood systems rather than in one director of extraction's head.
Vendors should be able to prove performance claims (e.g., via a working demo facility) rather than relying on best-case-scenario marketing numbers before an operator commits capital.

faq.question: Why isn't maximizing throughput the best goal for an extraction operation?
faq.answer: Throughput only measures activity, not performance. Pushing more biomass through faster can lower extraction efficiency and output quality, which keeps input costs the same or higher while reducing sellable output, ultimately hurting profitability even though throughput numbers look good.

faq.question: What is ingredient-based manufacturing in cannabis extraction?
faq.answer: It's an approach where extraction is focused on producing two core, highly standardized ingredients — 99.9% THCA isolate and High Terpene Extract (HTE) — instead of a single finished product. Those two ingredients can then be formulated on demand into any solvent-based concentrate to a tight specification.

faq.question: How does separating THCA and terpene extraction save money?
faq.answer: THCA is chemically identical regardless of biomass quality, so operators can use cheaper biomass to produce bulk THCA while only running smaller amounts of premium, connoisseur-grade biomass to capture the differentiating terpene (HTE) fraction, significantly lowering overall cost of goods.

faq.question: What's the risk of copying standardized SOPs from another facility?
faq.answer: Generalized SOPs without an understood 'why' behind each step lead to a less tightly run operation. Teams should know why they perform each step so they can diagnose problems or improve the process, rather than blindly following a procedure inherited from elsewhere.

faq.question: Why do extraction equipment setups often end up looking like a 'jungle gym' of quick-connect fixes?
faq.answer: Standardized, cookie-cutter turnkey systems get installed into very different operations and workflows, so operators start customizing them to solve immediate symptoms rather than root causes, leading to a patchwork of band-aid fixes that create new upstream and downstream problems.

faq.question: What should operators ask equipment vendors for before upgrading their system?
faq.answer: Operators should ask for proof of real-world performance — ideally seeing the equipment run at a demo facility — rather than relying on best-case-scenario marketing claims, since many vendors can't actually troubleshoot performance gaps once equipment underperforms specs.

faq.question: How does formulating products on demand help with shifting consumer trends?
faq.answer: Instead of mass-producing months of inventory based on a forecast that might miss, companies can make smaller batches as needed, quickly pivot formulations when demand shifts, and even test limited releases to front-run emerging trends without disrupting their core extraction workflow.

faq.question: Why is relying on one 'expert' director of extraction risky for a cannabis business?
faq.answer: If critical process knowledge lives only in one person's head, the business can't function properly if that person is unavailable. A scalable business documents and standardizes the reasoning behind its processes so operations continue regardless of personnel changes.
